question: Should we sunset the Google Forms submission flow mid-snapshot or wait for the next period?
restated: Decide whether to retire the Google Forms contribution-submission flow immediately, mid-snapshot, or hold the change until the next snapshot period begins.

round1.A:
The load-bearing assumption here is that a mid-snapshot cutover is mostly a tooling change. It is not — it is a trust event. Members who have half-submitted contributions in the old flow will experience the switch as the ground moving under a live process, and in a network whose strongest asset is member trust, that cost dwarfs two weeks of engineering convenience.

The case for waiting is stronger than it looks: nothing about the new flow's value depends on launching mid-period. The case for cutting over now rests on team momentum and a desire to stop maintaining two systems — real, but those are your incentives, not the members'. Notice also the recency bias: the new flow just passed QA, everyone is excited, and that excitement is doing argument-shaped work.

It is twelve months later and this failed: what happened? Submissions made in the final days of the old form were lost or double-counted in the migration, three members publicly questioned whether their contributions were recorded during the snapshot, and the program spent a quarter rebuilding confidence in the ledger itself.

What would change my mind: evidence that the old flow is actively corrupting data today, making waiting the riskier option.

Confidence: high
round1.B:
The real problem is not "when do we switch tools" — it is "how do we guarantee continuity of the contribution record across a system change." Restated that way, the timing question mostly answers itself.

Core truths this decision rests on. First: a snapshot period is an accounting boundary; changes inside an accounting period create reconciliation work by definition. Second: member trust in the contribution record is the program's foundational asset — it depreciates fast on ambiguity and rebuilds slowly. Third: the cost of waiting is bounded and known (a few weeks of dual maintenance); the cost of a mid-period migration error is unbounded and lands on trust.

The framework that fits is reversible-versus-irreversible doors. Waiting is a reversible choice — you can always accelerate later. A mid-snapshot cutover that miscounts even a handful of contributions is effectively irreversible, because the correction happens in public.

What is KNOWN: the new flow works; the period ends soon. What is ASSUMED: that migration is clean. What is UNKNOWABLE: which members are mid-submission right now.

Position: wait for the period boundary, and use the remaining weeks to rehearse the migration.

Confidence: high
round1.C:
Everyone is framing this as either-or; the bigger opportunity is to make the transition itself a visible contribution event. Three options beyond the ones presented.

One: launch the new flow now in parallel, read-only from the ledger's perspective — members can try it, feedback flows in, but the form of record stays Google Forms until the boundary. You bank adoption before the switch, and day one of the new period starts warm. The mechanism exists today: run both, count one.

Two: turn the cutover into a moment. Announce the retirement date, publish what improves, and invite members to stress-test the new flow during the overlap — the network's own members become the QA team, which is exactly the collaboration muscle the network says it wants to build.

Three, the asymmetric bet: a small "submission concierge" during the overlap window — any member unsure where to submit gets a human answer within a day. Downside capped at a few hours a week; upside is the trust story writes itself.

The first signal any of this is real: parallel-run signups in week one.

Confidence: medium
round1.D:
The obvious thing a stranger notices: you are asking whether to change the scoreboard in the middle of the game. In plain English — people are collecting credit for work under one set of rails, and you are deciding whether to swap the rails before the round ends. Said that plainly, it sounds like something you would only do in an emergency. Is this an emergency? Nothing in the question says so.

Questions I could not stop asking. Why does the switch feel urgent — is that a member need or a team preference? What happens to someone who submitted yesterday on the old form and checks their record next week? And who, by name, is the person a confused member asks?

Other fields handle this simply: banks do not change statement systems mid-cycle; leagues do not change scoring mid-season; even restaurants swap menus between services, not during them. The pattern everywhere is the same — change at the natural boundary, because boundaries are when expectations reset.

From the outside, waiting looks careful, not slow.

Confidence: medium
round1.E:
Position: wait, and treat the boundary date as a hard launch deadline. Here is the actual cost accounting.

Cut over mid-snapshot: migration script plus dual-write validation (est. 3–4 days), member comms drafted and translated for context (1 day), support load spike for the rest of the period (unbounded, likely 2–5 hours/week), plus reconciliation of any submissions caught in flight — the item most likely to slip, because it depends on member behavior you do not control.

Wait for the boundary: two to three weeks of dual maintenance (est. 1–2 hours/week), one announcement, one clean cutover on a date members already treat as a reset.

The critical path if you wait: freeze old-form changes now → publish the retirement date this week → dry-run the migration on a copy of the data (half a day) → cut over at 00:00 on day one of the new period → archive the form.

Kill criteria: if the dry run surfaces data problems twice in a row, the new flow is not ready regardless of timing. Checkpoint: one week before the boundary, go/no-go with whoever owns member support.

First concrete move: send the retirement-date announcement draft for review tomorrow morning.

Confidence: high

round2.A:
On my fellow advisors: I concede to Advisor E that the bounded cost accounting settles the economics — the wait is cheap and the cutover risk is not. I build on Advisor B's framing: the accounting-boundary argument is the strongest version of my trust concern, stated structurally. Advisor D's scoreboard image is the same point again from the member's chair; three routes to one conclusion is signal, not redundancy. To Advisor C I offer a partial rebuttal: the parallel-run is genuinely good, but only if the form of record is unambiguous every single day — a soft launch that muddies where submissions count would recreate the exact failure I opened with.

Revised position: my original objection stands, sharpened. The plan survives only in the wait-for-boundary shape. What the council has adequately answered: whether waiting is timid — it is not; it is the only option whose failure modes are recoverable.

The one objection still standing: nobody has yet named the owner of the migration dry-run. An unowned rehearsal is a rehearsal that does not happen.

Confidence: high
For the Chairman: the mid-snapshot option's failure mode is public and irreversible; no argument presented touches that asymmetry.
round2.B:
Advisor A and I converged independently on irreversibility, which strengthens my confidence in the frame. I concede to Advisor C one real improvement: a parallel run does not violate the accounting boundary as long as the form of record is explicit — my second core truth survives intact if the ledger reads from exactly one source per period. I build on Advisor E's critical path: it is the operational cash-out of the reversible-door framework, and the dry-run step is where the ASSUMED column (clean migration) becomes KNOWN. Advisor D's cross-domain examples are analogies, so I checked the mechanics: statements, seasons, and menus all share the property that the boundary is when reconciliation happens anyway — the mechanics transfer.

Revised position, unchanged in direction and firmer in shape: hold the cutover to the period boundary; run the new flow in parallel as a non-record trial; rehearse the migration before the boundary.

Confidence: high
For the Chairman: the decision is not timing but continuity of record — and continuity is only guaranteed at the boundary.
round2.C:
I concede the center of gravity: Advisors A, B, and E have convinced me that the form of record must not move mid-period — my parallel-run option only works with a bright line under it, and I have redrawn it that way. This was correct discipline, not small thinking.

But I hold the bigger frame: everyone else is optimizing the defensive case, and there is real upside being left unpriced. The overlap window is a free trial period with a built-in audience; the retirement announcement is a chance to show members the program improving in the open. Advisor E's concierge-adjacent checkpoint makes my third option cheaper than I priced it — fold the concierge into existing support rotation and the marginal cost rounds to zero.

Revised position: wait for the boundary AND run the warm-start plan — parallel trial (clearly non-record), a dated retirement announcement that reads as an upgrade story, and a named human for confused members. The mechanism for all three exists today.

Confidence: medium, raised toward high on the combined plan
For the Chairman: waiting and ambition are not in tension — the boundary date is also a launch date.
round2.D:
My obvious observation held up well: four of us, from completely different directions, landed on "do not change the scoreboard mid-game." When the careful one, the structural one, and the operational one all agree with the naive read, the naive read was probably just right.

Where I push back: some of my colleagues are speaking fluent insider again. "Dual-write validation," "form of record," "reconciliation window" — fine, but the member-facing version of this plan must be one sentence long: "submit here until the period ends; submit there starting next period." If the plan cannot be said that simply to a member, it is not done. Advisor C's trial-period idea passes this test, which is why I build on it — trying the new thing with no stakes is how normal people learn tools everywhere else in life.

One question never got asked: has anyone told the members who use the old form most? They will notice first.

Confidence: medium, leaning high on the wait
For the Chairman: the plan is ready when it fits in one sentence a member would actually read.
round2.E:
Pricing the council's proposals. Advisor C's warm-start plan: parallel trial plus announcement plus named support contact — call it 2 days of setup and 1–2 hours a week during overlap. Cheap, and it converts dead waiting time into adoption. I fold it into the plan. Advisor B's dry-run requirement: half a day, already on my critical path, now with a named acceptance test — zero unexplained diffs between old-form data and migrated data. Advisor A asked who owns the rehearsal: correct catch. The plan does not leave this room without an owner slot, even if the name is filled in Monday.

Revised plan, consolidated: (1) tomorrow — announce the retirement date, one member-readable sentence up top; (2) this week — open the new flow as a clearly labeled non-record trial; (3) by the checkpoint — migration dry-run with the zero-diff test, owner named; (4) boundary day — cut over, archive the form, concierge window for two weeks.

Kill criteria unchanged: two failed dry-runs means the new flow waits a period, no debate.

Confidence: high
For the Chairman: the wait costs almost nothing and buys a rehearsal; take it.

verdict:
## The question
Retire the Google Forms submission flow mid-snapshot, or hold the cutover to the next period boundary?

## Where the council converged
All five advisors, from independent directions, reached the same core position: do not move the form of record mid-period. The council also converged on three supporting points — the cost of waiting is small and bounded; the cost of a mid-period migration error is public and effectively irreversible; and the period boundary is a natural reset members already understand.

## Live disagreements
The live tension is emphasis, not direction. Advisor C maintains the council is under-pricing the upside of the overlap window and wants the transition run as a visible upgrade story; Advisors A and B accept this only with a bright line — the ledger reads from exactly one source per period. Advisor D holds that the plan is not done until it is one member-readable sentence, a bar the technical plan has not yet met.

## The verdict
Wait for the period boundary — and use the wait. This is not the cautious option; it is the option whose failure modes are recoverable. Adopt the consolidated plan: announce the retirement date now, open the new flow immediately as a clearly labeled non-record trial, rehearse the migration with a zero-diff acceptance test, and cut over at the boundary. The argument quality was one-sided: no advisor produced a reason the switch must happen mid-period that survived the asymmetry of the risks.

## First step
Monday morning: draft the retirement-date announcement with the one-sentence member version up top ("Submit here until the period ends; submit in the new flow starting next period"), and name the owner of the migration dry-run in the same message.

## Biggest risk
Drift during the overlap window — members submitting into the trial flow believing it counts. The "non-record trial" label must be unmissable, and the concierge answer must be a person, not a doc.

## Unresolved questions
Whether the heaviest users of the old form have been consulted directly; and whether the new flow's own submission data model has been reviewed against the next period's contribution categories, which the council could not assess from the information given.

followup_example.q: What if the new flow isn't ready by the boundary?
followup_example.a: Then the old form runs one more full period — cleanly, with the retirement date moved once and announced once. The council's kill criteria already cover this: two failed migration dry-runs means the new flow waits, no debate. What you must not do is let the boundary pressure you into a partial cutover; a half-migrated period recreates exactly the irreversible failure mode the council voted to avoid. Advisor E's checkpoint — go/no-go one week before the boundary with member support in the room — is where this call gets made.
